title: Tasks, @MainActor and "which thread am I on?"
summary: `@MainActor` means "this code always runs on the main thread". A `Task` is a unit of async work. Together they replace most `DispatchQueue.main.async` calls.
body: **In simple words:** UI must be touched only on the main thread. Marking a class or function `@MainActor` makes the compiler guarantee that. If you call it from somewhere else, you must `await`, and Swift hops to the main thread for you.

**Typical setup:** view models and UI classes are `@MainActor`. Heavy work (parsing, image processing) runs in a function marked `@concurrent` (Swift 6.2) or `nonisolated`, or inside an actor, and the result comes back to the main actor.

**Task basics:** `Task { }` starts async work. It keeps running until it finishes even if you drop the handle - so keep the handle and call `cancel()` when the screen goes away. SwiftUI `.task { }` cancels automatically when the view disappears.
**Priorities:** `.high/.userInitiated`, `.medium`, `.low/.utility`, `.background`. If a high-priority task awaits a low-priority one, Swift raises the low one's priority (priority escalation).
**Swift 6.2 default isolation:** a module can choose `MainActor` as the default, so most UI code needs no annotations; you only mark the exceptions that should run in the background.
**`MainActor.assumeIsolated { }`** tells the compiler "I know this callback is already on main" (e.g. some UIKit delegate). It crashes if you are wrong, so use it carefully.
keyPoints: `@MainActor` = compile-time guarantee that code runs on the main thread.
Calling main-actor code from elsewhere needs `await`; Swift does the hop.
Unstructured `Task {}` is not cancelled automatically; store and cancel it, or use SwiftUI `.task`.
Offload CPU-heavy work with `@concurrent` (6.2) or an actor, then return to the main actor to update state.
Task priority escalates automatically when a higher-priority task awaits a lower one.

mistakes: Wrapping everything in `DispatchQueue.main.async` inside async code instead of using `@MainActor`.
Using `Task.detached` to "go to background" by habit - it loses priority and cancellation context.
Forgetting to cancel long-running tasks when a screen closes.
followups: **How do you check you are on main?** `MainActor.assertIsolated()` or `dispatchPrecondition(condition: .onQueue(.main))` in debug.
**What is a global actor?** An actor that can isolate code anywhere via an attribute, like `@MainActor`; you can define your own (e.g. `@DatabaseActor`).
**What does `nonisolated` mean?** The member does not belong to the actor, so it can be called without `await` but cannot touch the actor's mutable state.
